Hello again,

I'm interested in performing a genomic SEM factor analysis (and eventually generating summary stats).   I've identified an EFA model and would like to perform CFA (without SNPs).    Having some difficulty when attempting to run the CFA.   I checked that all of the variables in the Lavaan model are named correctly, so perhaps I'm mis-specifying the analysis?

Any help would be appreciated,
Thanks

##  Generate covariance matrices.
LDSCoutput <- ldsc(traits=traits, sample.prev=sample_prev, population.prev=pop_prev, ld, wld, trait.names=trait_names)
k<-nrow(LDSCoutput$S)
SE<-matrix(0, k, k)
SE[lower.tri(SE,diag=TRUE)] <-sqrt(diag(LDSCoutput$V))

# Explore the EFA
require(Matrix)
Ssmooth<-as.matrix((nearPD(LDSCoutput$S, corr = FALSE))$mat)
require(stats)
.

modelx <-'F1 =~ NA*PsyBIP + PsyMDD + PsySZ + PsyRiskTolerance
          F2 =~ NA*PsyOCDPGC + PsyTSYu + MedCeliacDubuois + MedTDBradfield + PsyAN + PsyADHDDemontis
          F3 =~ NA*PsyNEUR + PsyAnxietyGADScoreLevey + IntCognitiveProcessingLee + PsyADHDDemontis
          F4 =~ NA*MedUC + MedCD + MedPSCSunGu
          F5 =~ NA*MedTDBradfield + MedHYPO + PsyOCDPGC + MedPSCSunGu + MedVitiligoJin + PsyADHDDemontis
          F6 =~ NA*MedSLEBentham + MedPBC + MedRAOkada
          F7 =~ NA*MedCeliacDubuois + MedHYPO + PsyOCDPGC
          F1 ~~ F2 + F3 + F4 + F5 + F6 + F7
          F2 ~~ F3 + F4 + F5 + F6 + F7
          F3 ~~ F4 + F5 + F6 + F7
          F4 ~~ F5 + F6 + F7
          F5 ~~ F6 + F7
          F6 ~~ F7'

model_out<-usermodel(covstruc = LDSCoutput,
           estimation = "DWLS",
            model = modelx,
            CFIcalc = TRUE,
            std.lv <http://std.lv/> = TRUE,
            imp_cov = FALSE)

Hi Dan,

Based on the error it looks like the "fake" model used to determine ordering of the sampling covariance matrix used for CFI estimation wasn't converging. I've added in code to force that fake model to converge if you want to re-install Genomic SEM and restart R and give it a try.

It sounds like for previous runs you were excluding certain variables entirely based on the loadings? I ask largely because that would explain why the error you posted wasn't coming up in those cases. As far as recommendations for picking up loadings, it's really hard to give a rule of thumb on that end. I think it can kind of depend how much your variables generally hang together, so if you've got a lot of variables with loadings of > .5 and one or two loners of < .2 then you might make a different judgement call about cut-offs then if you have a set of variables all with loadings of ~.3. With that said, I've used a cut-off of .35 in my most recent project.

-Andrew

messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I'm working through a userGWAS and am having somewhat of a hard time determining the specifications for the sumstats function. My first question is should we be specifying OLS=T even if the model is an LMM? Or does the OLS specification just refer to any linear, continuous GWAS? And relatedly how much of an issue are LMMs with GSEM? I know BOLT-LMM employs the leave-one-chromosome-out method, but I'm not totally sure if the following text is saying MLMe is ok but MLMi (in Yang's terms) isn't? And if we should not be using BOLT-LMM generated sumstats with GSEM is there a reference for that?

"Another issue is the use of "linear mixed models" (LMM) in GWAS. These models are used to guard against populations stratification, and cryptic relatedness between study participants. The pitfalls of, and opportunities afforded by, these models are discussed by Yang et al (2014) <https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC3989144/>. These models guard against cryptic relatedness in a sample by determining the relationship between all pairs of subjects in a study, and fitting a random effect based on this information. Important for you to know is that there are two types of mixed models. The first type, which Yang et al. call "MLMi," uses all SNPs in determining the relationship between subjects, including the SNP that is entered as a fixed effect into the model. This type of mixed model is best considered incompatible with GenomicSEM and LD score regression in general. The second type of mixed model, which Yang et al. call "MLMe," determines cryptic relatedness between pairs of participants based on all chromosomes but the one on which the SNP considered as a fixed effect is located. This leads to a downward biased estimate of heritability in LD score regression and therefore also in GenomicSEM."

Thanks!
Claire

messages.subject: Re: OLS/ LMMs
messages.subject_clean: OLS/ LMMs
messages.body_plain:
Hi Claire,

Great question! If it was BOLT-LMM for a continuous phenotype than the correct specification would be OLS=T. I would say it is a little unclear how best to deal with BOLT-LMM results in Genomic SEM at the moment, but I can make some general suggestions based on what we’ve observed.

1. If you go to the referenced Yang et al. (2014) paper "Advantages and pitfalls in the application of mixed-model association methods" they examine the relationship between the chi-square from traditional linear regression and two different types of mixed model approaches: MLMe and MLMi. In Figure 1 of this paper you can see that MLMi leads to a clear deflation in the chi-square statistic relative to linear regression, and will consequently result in a deflation in the heritability estimate obtained from LDSC and is therefore not appropriate for LDSC. Not super relevant because most packages developed recently uses MLMe, including SAIGE and BOLT-LMM. The relationship between the linear regression and MLMe is not exactly 1, but we've generally found for traits with h2 < 50% and participant sample sizes < 400k that BOLT-LMM and traditional linear regression LDSC results are very similar when comparing estimates obtained from the same participant samples and phenotypes. So when running a model without individual SNP effects using the usermodel function, estimates from MLMe (and consequently BOLT-LMM) seem to be fine to use in Genomic SEM.

2. While the heritability estimate should be very consistent between MLMe and traditional linear models, Loh et al. (2018) find in a paper titled “Mixed-model association for biobank-scale datasets,” that it is the univariate LDSC intercept in BOLT-LMM that is the most difficult to interpret as it will “rise above 1 with increasing sample size and heritability.” This LDSC univariate intercept is used in the sampling covariance matrix for the multivariate GWAS to account for confounding, and so BOLT-LMM estimates will produce an inflated LDSC intercept and consequently conservative multivariate GWAS estimates. Since BOLT-LMM controls for sample structure that would otherwise be captured by the LDSC univariate intercept, for BOLT-LMM traits I would say it is most sensible to set the LDSC intercept to 1. For right now, this can be achieved by manually setting the diagonals of the intercept matrix (the third part of the LSC output named I) for the BOLT-LMM traits to 1.

Best,

  Andrew

> Hi,

> I'm working through a userGWAS and am having somewhat of a hard time determining the specifications for the sumstats function. My first question is should we be specifying OLS=T even if the model is an LMM? Or does the OLS specification just refer to any linear, continuous GWAS? And relatedly how much of an issue are LMMs with GSEM? I know BOLT-LMM employs the leave-one-chromosome-out method, but I'm not totally sure if the following text is saying MLMe is ok but MLMi (in Yang's terms) isn't? And if we should not be using BOLT-LMM generated sumstats with GSEM is there a reference for that?
>
> "Another issue is the use of "linear mixed models" (LMM) in GWAS. These models are used to guard against populations stratification, and cryptic relatedness between study participants. The pitfalls of, and opportunities afforded by, these models are discussed by Yang et al (2014) <https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC3989144/>. These models guard against cryptic relatedness in a sample by determining the relationship between all pairs of subjects in a study, and fitting a random effect based on this information. Important for you to know is that there are two types of mixed models. The first type, which Yang et al. call "MLMi," uses all SNPs in determining the relationship between subjects, including the SNP that is entered as a fixed effect into the model. This type of mixed model is best considered incompatible with GenomicSEM and LD score regression in general. The second type of mixed model, which Yang et al. call "MLMe," determines cryptic relatedness between pairs of participants based on all chromosomes but the one on which the SNP considered as a fixed effect is located. This leads to a downward biased estimate of heritability in LD score regression and therefore also in GenomicSEM."

> Hi Claire,

> Great question! If it was BOLT-LMM for a continuous phenotype than the correct specification would be OLS=T. I would say it is a little unclear how best to deal with BOLT-LMM results in Genomic SEM at the moment, but I can make some general suggestions based on what we’ve observed.
>
> 1. If you go to the referenced Yang et al. (2014) paper "Advantages and pitfalls in the application of mixed-model association methods" they examine the relationship between the chi-square from traditional linear regression and two different types of mixed model approaches: MLMe and MLMi. In Figure 1 of this paper you can see that MLMi leads to a clear deflation in the chi-square statistic relative to linear regression, and will consequently result in a deflation in the heritability estimate obtained from LDSC and is therefore not appropriate for LDSC. Not super relevant because most packages developed recently uses MLMe, including SAIGE and BOLT-LMM. The relationship between the linear regression and MLMe is not exactly 1, but we've generally found for traits with h2 < 50% and participant sample sizes < 400k that BOLT-LMM and traditional linear regression LDSC results are very similar when comparing estimates obtained from the same participant samples and phenotypes. So when running a model without individual SNP effects using the usermodel function, estimates from MLMe (and consequently BOLT-LMM) seem to be fine to use in Genomic SEM.
>
> 2. While the heritability estimate should be very consistent between MLMe and traditional linear models, Loh et al. (2018) find in a paper titled “Mixed-model association for biobank-scale datasets,” that it is the univariate LDSC intercept in BOLT-LMM that is the most difficult to interpret as it will “rise above 1 with increasing sample size and heritability.” This LDSC univariate intercept is used in the sampling covariance matrix for the multivariate GWAS to account for confounding, and so BOLT-LMM estimates will produce an inflated LDSC intercept and consequently conservative multivariate GWAS estimates. Since BOLT-LMM controls for sample structure that would otherwise be captured by the LDSC univariate intercept, for BOLT-LMM traits I would say it is most sensible to set the LDSC intercept to 1. For right now, this can be achieved by manually setting the diagonals of the intercept matrix (the third part of the LSC output named I) for the BOLT-LMM traits to 1.
>
> Best,
